description_full: e.l.f. Beauty, Inc., a beauty company, provides cosmetics and skin care products worldwide. The company offers eye, lip, face, and skin care products. It offers products under the e.l.f. Cosmetics, e.l.f. Skin, Well People, Naturium, and Rhode brand names. The company sells its products through national and international retailers and direct-to-consumer through its e-commerce channel. The company was formerly known as J.A. Cosmetics Holdings, Inc. and changed its name to e.l.f. Beauty, Inc. in April 2016. e.l.f. Beauty, Inc. was founded in 2004 and is headquartered in Oakland, California.

CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: e.l.f. Beauty, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $6.9B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +41% over the past three years and +22% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 10% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 65% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $190M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 8.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.6%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.9% of the shares.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 34% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 65% and a beta of 1.22, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.12 vs 5y 1.45), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $139.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $12.89 (margin of safety -801%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.86 to $21.99 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 81.8 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 22.2 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 36.1 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 77% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $120 on average, 3% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 10.0%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.76).
It runs a 65% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow, or 6% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 2% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.3% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($289.7M of cash against $809.3M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.2, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 132 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 41.4% over 3 years, 38.8% over 5 years and 21.7% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
At current returns, reinvesting 68% of profits supports about 10.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 52.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 45, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 82.4% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.9%, and institutions hold 97%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (21 sales, net $16.1M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.6% (0.6% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 2.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 849 employees, each generates about $1.9M of revenue, 3.8x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 21.7% a year.
That works out to $224K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.4M (1x revenue per employee).
